hints: Sort first so duplicate values become adjacent.
Fix one value, then search the remaining suffix with two pointers.
For each i, move left or right by comparing nums[i] + nums[left] + nums[right] with zero; skip repeated values.
3sum.explanation: Sorting followed by a linear two-pointer scan for each fixed index is quadratic; excluding sort storage, pointers are constant space.

hints: A selling day only needs the cheapest earlier price.
Track a running minimum and the best profit seen so far.
For each price, update profit from price - minimum, then update the minimum.
best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock.explanation: One pass stores only the minimum price and best profit.

hints: Area is limited by the shorter boundary.
Start at both ends and move the shorter side inward.
Compute min(height[l], height[r]) * (r-l); advancing the taller side cannot improve the limiting height.
container-with-most-water.explanation: Each pointer moves inward at most n times and no auxiliary collection is needed.

hints: Ask whether a value has appeared before.
Use a set while scanning.
Return true when insertion finds an existing value; otherwise finish after one pass.
contains-duplicate.explanation: Expected set lookup is constant time per element and the set may hold every value.

hints: At least one side of the midpoint remains sorted.
Compare the midpoint with the rightmost value.
If nums[mid] > nums[right], the minimum is right of mid; otherwise keep mid and discard its right suffix.
find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array.explanation: Binary search halves the interval while retaining only indices.

hints: A negative value can turn the smallest product into the largest.
Track both maximum and minimum products ending at each position.
For x, compute max(x, x*oldMax, x*oldMin) and the matching minimum, then update the answer.
maximum-product-subarray.explanation: The dynamic state is reduced to two running products.

hints: A negative prefix should not burden the next subarray.
Track the best sum ending exactly at the current element.
Set current = max(x, current+x) and update the global maximum.
maximum-subarray.explanation: Kadane's recurrence uses one pass and constant state.

hints: Separate contributions from the left and right.
Store prefix products in the answer, then multiply by a running suffix product.
Forward: answer[i]=prefix; prefix*=nums[i]. Backward: answer[i]*=suffix; suffix*=nums[i].
product-of-array-except-self.explanation: Two linear passes use the output array plus constant extra state.

hints: One half around every midpoint is normally sorted.
Identify the sorted half, then decide whether the target lies inside it.
Use binary search; retain the sorted half only when its boundary range contains target, otherwise search the other half.
search-in-rotated-sorted-array.explanation: Each comparison removes half the remaining range.

hints: For each number, think about the value still needed.
Store previously seen values with their indices.
At index i, check target-nums[i] in the map before inserting nums[i].
two-sum.explanation: A hash map gives expected constant lookup per element and may store n entries.

hints: Relate i to a smaller number whose answer is known.
Removing the lowest set bit produces i & (i-1).
Use bits[i] = bits[i & (i-1)] + 1 for i from 1 through n.
counting-bits.explanation: Each output is computed in constant time; the returned table has n+1 entries.

hints: Pair every expected index with every present value.
XOR cancels equal numbers without overflow.
Initialize result=n, then XOR each index and nums[index].
missing-number.explanation: One pass and one XOR accumulator suffice.

hints: Remove one set bit per iteration.
n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit.
Loop while n != 0, replace n with n & (n-1), and increment the count.
number-of-1-bits.explanation: The input has fixed machine width, so at most 32 bit-clearing steps are required.

hints: Build the result one bit at a time.
Read the low bit of n and append it to the shifted result.
Repeat 32 times: result=(result<<1)|(n&1), then n>>=1.
reverse-bits.explanation: Exactly 32 iterations and two integer accumulators are used.

hints: Separate addition into sum-without-carry and carry.
XOR adds bits; AND followed by a left shift creates carries.
Repeat a,b = a XOR b, (a AND b)<<1 under a fixed-width mask until carry is zero.
sum-of-two-integers.explanation: Fixed-width integers require a bounded number of carry propagations.

hints: The final move came from one or two steps below.
This is the Fibonacci recurrence.
Iterate next = oneBack + twoBack through step n using two variables.
climbing-stairs.explanation: Each step is computed once with two rolling values.

hints: Build answers for smaller amounts first.
Let dp[a] be the fewest coins needed for amount a.
Initialize dp[0]=0; for each amount and coin<=amount, minimize dp[amount-coin]+1.
coin-change.explanation: Every amount considers every denomination and the table has amount+1 cells.

hints: Order matters, so choose the final number for each total.
Let dp[t] count ordered sequences summing to t.
Set dp[0]=1; for each total, sum dp[total-num] for every usable num.
combination-sum-iv.explanation: Each target subtotal scans n numbers and stores one count.

hints: A valid decoding ends with one digit or two digits.
Track ways for the previous two prefixes.
At position i, add previous ways if digit is 1-9 and two-back ways if the two-digit value is 10-26.
decode-ways.explanation: One pass uses two rolling prefix counts.

hints: At each house, compare taking it with skipping it.
Taking the current value requires the best result two positions back.
Update currentBest=max(previousBest, twoBack+value) while rolling the two states.
house-robber.explanation: The recurrence is evaluated once per house with constant state.

hints: The first and last houses cannot both be selected.
Solve two linear ranges: exclude the first or exclude the last.
Run the ordinary House Robber recurrence on nums[1:] and nums[:-1], then take the maximum.
house-robber-ii.explanation: Two linear constant-space passes cover the circular cases.

hints: Track how far the processed prefix can reach.
If an index lies beyond that reach, it is impossible.
Scan left to right, updating farthest=max(farthest,i+nums[i]); succeed once farthest reaches the end.
jump-game.explanation: The greedy frontier is updated once per index.

hints: Compare prefixes of both strings.
Matching final characters extend a smaller common subsequence; nonmatches drop one side.
Use dp[i][j]=1+dp[i-1][j-1] on a match, else max(dp[i-1][j],dp[i][j-1]).
longest-common-subsequence.explanation: The DP visits every character pair and can retain only the previous row.

hints: Maintain the smallest possible tail for each subsequence length.
Binary-search the first tail not smaller than the current value.
Replace that tail, or append when the value exceeds all tails; the tails length is the answer.
longest-increasing-subsequence.explanation: Each of n values performs one binary search in the tails array.

hints: A cell is reached from above or left.
One row is enough if it is updated left to right.
Initialize the row to ones; for each later row set dp[col] += dp[col-1].
unique-paths.explanation: Every grid cell contributes once and one row is retained.

hints: Ask whether each prefix can be segmented.
A prefix is valid when an earlier valid prefix is followed by a dictionary word.
Set dp[0]=true; for end positions, try starts and mark dp[end] when dp[start] and s[start:end] is a word.
word-break.explanation: There are quadratically many prefix splits and n+1 boolean states.

hints: Adjacent sorted words reveal the first differing character's order.
Build a directed graph, while detecting the invalid longer-prefix case.
Add one edge for each adjacent first difference, then topologically sort all characters; a cycle means no order.
alien-dictionary.explanation: Each input character and graph edge is processed a constant number of times.

hints: Each original node needs exactly one cloned counterpart.
Use a map from original nodes to clones during DFS or BFS.
Create the clone before traversing neighbors, then append recursively obtained neighbor clones.
clone-graph.explanation: Every vertex and edge is visited once; the map and traversal hold vertices.

hints: Prerequisites form a directed graph.
Completion is possible exactly when the graph has no cycle.
Compute indegrees, repeatedly remove zero-indegree courses, and verify that all courses were removed.
course-schedule.explanation: Topological sorting scans all courses and prerequisite edges.

hints: A tree is connected and has no cycle.
n vertices in a tree must have exactly n-1 edges.
Reject a wrong edge count, then DFS/BFS from one node and confirm all n vertices are visited.
graph-valid-tree.explanation: The adjacency list and traversal cover every vertex and edge.

hints: Only begin counting at the start of a run.
A number starts a run when number-1 is absent from the set.
Put values in a set; for each run start, advance while consecutive successors exist and track the maximum length.
longest-consecutive-sequence.explanation: Each value participates in at most one run scan on average.

hints: Each new traversal discovers one component.
Build adjacency lists, then start DFS/BFS from every unvisited vertex.
Increment the count before exploring an unvisited start and mark all reachable vertices.
number-of-connected-components-in-an-und.explanation: The graph representation and traversals process each vertex and edge.

hints: Every unvisited land cell can start one island traversal.
Flood-fill connected land in four directions.
Scan the grid; on '1', increment the count and DFS/BFS while marking reached land.
number-of-islands.explanation: Every cell is visited at most once; traversal storage can cover the grid.

hints: Reverse the direction: start from each ocean rather than every cell.
From an ocean, move to neighbors of equal or greater height.
Run flood fills from Pacific borders and Atlantic borders; return the intersection of reachable cells.
pacific-atlantic-water-flow.explanation: Two traversals visit each cell at most once and store two reachability sets.

hints: Intervals before the new one and after it need no merging.
Append disjoint left intervals, merge overlaps into the new range, then append the rest.
Advance while end<newStart; merge while start<=newEnd; append the merged interval and remaining suffix.
insert-interval.explanation: A single pass builds the returned interval list.

hints: Only adjacent meetings matter after ordering by start time.
Sort intervals by start.
If any current start is less than the previous end, the schedule overlaps.
meeting-rooms.explanation: Sorting dominates; the overlap scan uses constant auxiliary state.

hints: A room becomes reusable when its meeting ends.
Sort starts and ends separately or keep active end times in a min-heap.
Sweep start times; release every end <= start, then allocate a room and track the maximum active count.
meeting-rooms-ii.explanation: Sorting or heap operations cost logarithmic time per meeting.

hints: Ordering by start makes possible overlaps adjacent.
Keep one current merged interval.
If the next start <= current end, extend the end; otherwise emit current and begin a new interval.
merge-intervals.explanation: Sorting dominates and the output may contain every interval.

hints: Keeping intervals that finish early leaves the most room.
Sort by end and greedily retain compatible intervals.
Count an interval as removed when start<lastEnd; otherwise keep it and update lastEnd=end.
non-overlapping-intervals.explanation: End-time sorting dominates the constant-state greedy scan.

hints: Use two walkers with different speeds.
A fast pointer eventually meets a slow pointer if a cycle exists.
Advance slow by one and fast by two until they meet or fast reaches null.
linked-list-cycle.explanation: The pointers traverse a linear number of links with constant storage.

hints: At any moment, only the smallest remaining head can be next.
Keep current list heads in a min-heap.
Pop the smallest node, append it, and push its successor until the heap is empty.
merge-k-sorted-lists.explanation: Each of N nodes enters a heap containing at most k heads.

hints: Compare only the two current heads.
Append the smaller head and advance its list.
Use a dummy head, loop while both lists remain, then attach the nonempty suffix.
merge-two-sorted-lists.explanation: Every node is linked once with constant pointer state.

hints: Create a gap of n nodes between two pointers.
A dummy node simplifies removing the head.
Move fast n steps from dummy, advance both until fast.next is null, then bypass slow.next.
remove-nth-node-from-end-of-list.explanation: Two pointers make one linear traversal.

hints: The target order alternates from the front and back.
Find the midpoint, reverse the second half, then merge alternating nodes.
Use slow/fast pointers, reverse after slow, and weave first/second pointers until the second half ends.
reorder-list.explanation: Three linear pointer passes modify links in place.

hints: Preserve the next node before changing a link.
Carry previous and current pointers.
Loop: next=current.next; current.next=previous; previous=current; current=next.
reverse-linked-list.explanation: Each link is reversed once with three pointers.

hints: A 90-degree rotation can be decomposed into two simple transforms.
Transpose across the main diagonal, then reverse each row.
Swap matrix[r][c] with matrix[c][r] for c>r, then reverse rows in place.
rotate-image.explanation: Each matrix cell is touched a constant number of times in place.

hints: Use the matrix's first row and column as marker storage.
Remember separately whether the first row and first column originally contain zero.
Mark row/column headers for interior zeros, clear interiors, then clear the first row/column from saved flags.
set-matrix-zeroes.explanation: A few full-grid passes reuse existing cells as markers.

hints: Maintain the unvisited rectangle's four boundaries.
Traverse top, right, bottom, and left, shrinking after each side.
Guard bottom and left traversals after shrinking so single rows or columns are not repeated.
spiral-matrix.explanation: Every cell is emitted exactly once; boundary indices are constant space.

hints: A path cannot reuse a cell.
Start backtracking wherever the first character matches.
Temporarily mark the current cell, try four neighbors for the next character, then restore it on return.
word-search.explanation: Each start explores up to four choices per word character; recursion depth is L.

hints: A separator alone is ambiguous when strings may contain it.
Prefix each string with its length and a delimiter.
Encode as length#content; decode by reading digits to #, then consume exactly that many characters.
encode-and-decode-strings.explanation: Encoding and decoding inspect each payload character once and create output of proportional size.

hints: Anagrams share a canonical signature.
Use sorted characters or a fixed letter-frequency tuple as a map key.
Compute the signature for each word and append it to that key's list.
group-anagrams.explanation: Frequency signatures scan K characters per word and grouped output stores all characters.

hints: Every palindrome has a center.
Expand around each character and each gap.
For each of 2n-1 centers, move outward while characters match and retain the longest bounds.
longest-palindromic-substring.explanation: Each center may expand across the string; only best indices are stored.

hints: Within a window, all non-majority characters need replacement.
A window is valid when length - highestFrequency <= k.
Expand right while updating counts; shrink left when replacements exceed k and track the largest window.
longest-repeating-character-replacement.explanation: Both window pointers move forward once; the alphabet count is bounded.

hints: Maintain a window containing no duplicate character.
Remember the most recent index of each character.
Move left to max(left,lastSeen[ch]+1), update lastSeen, and maximize right-left+1.
longest-substring-without-repeating-char.explanation: One pass stores at most one index per distinct character.

hints: Track how many required character counts are currently satisfied.
Expand until the window is valid, then shrink while preserving validity.
Use need/window counts and a formed counter; record the shortest valid bounds before decrementing the left character.
minimum-window-substring.explanation: Each pointer crosses the source once and maps store relevant character counts.

hints: Count palindromes by their centers.
Use both character centers and gaps.
Expand while the two characters match and increment the total for every valid expansion.
palindromic-substrings.explanation: There are O(n) centers and each can expand O(n) positions.

hints: Equal strings must have equal character counts.
Increment counts for one string and decrement for the other.
Reject unequal lengths, update one frequency map, then verify every count returns to zero.
valid-anagram.explanation: Both strings are scanned once and counts depend on the alphabet.

hints: Ignore characters that are not alphanumeric.
Compare normalized characters from both ends.
Advance each pointer past punctuation, compare lowercase values, and move inward.
valid-palindrome.explanation: Two pointers inspect each character at most once without building a copy.

hints: An opener must match the next closer in reverse order.
Use a stack of expected closing characters.
Push the matching closer for every opener; for a closer, require it equals the stack top; finish with an empty stack.
valid-parentheses.explanation: Every bracket is pushed or popped once and the stack can hold n openers.

hints: Process nodes in breadth-first layers.
At each iteration, capture the queue's current size.
Pop exactly that many nodes into one level while enqueuing their children.
binary-tree-level-order-traversal.explanation: Every node enters the queue once; a level may contain O(n) nodes.

hints: A path passed to a parent can use at most one child branch.
Postorder returns the best downward gain while updating a global path through each node.
Use max(0,leftGain) and max(0,rightGain); update answer with node+both, return node+max(one branch).
binary-tree-maximum-path-sum.explanation: Postorder visits every node once and recursion follows tree height.

hints: Preorder identifies each subtree's root first.
Inorder locates the boundary between left and right subtrees.
Map inorder values to indices, advance a preorder pointer, and recurse on inorder ranges left and right of the root.
construct-binary-tree-from-preorder-and-.explanation: The index map avoids repeated searches; each node is constructed once.

hints: Each edge represents one character.
Nodes need child links and an end-of-word marker.
Insert by creating missing child nodes; search/prefix walk existing links, with search also requiring the terminal marker.
implement-trie-prefix-tree.explanation: Each operation follows L characters; stored nodes are bounded by all inserted characters.

hints: Ordinary letters follow one trie edge; '.' can follow any edge.
Use a trie and recursive search for wildcard positions.
At '.', recursively try every child for the next index; at the end require the word marker.
design-add-and-search-words-data-structu.explanation: A wildcard-heavy search can branch across the alphabet; the trie stores inserted characters.

hints: Every node performs the same local swap.
Swap left and right, then invert both children.
Return null at an empty node; recursively assign node.left=invert(oldRight) and node.right=invert(oldLeft).
invert-binary-tree.explanation: Every node is visited once and recursion depth follows tree height.

hints: Inorder traversal of a BST is sorted.
Stop after visiting k nodes in inorder order.
Use an explicit stack: descend left, pop/count, then move to the right child until count reaches k.
kth-smallest-element-in-a-bst.explanation: The traversal descends the height and visits only the first k sorted nodes.

hints: BST ordering tells which side contains both targets.
If both values are below the current node go left; if both are above go right.
The first node where the targets split sides, or equals a target, is the LCA.
lowest-common-ancestor-of-a-binary-searc.explanation: One root-to-node path is followed iteratively.

hints: A node's depth depends on the deeper child.
Use 1 + max(leftDepth, rightDepth).
Return zero for null; recursively compute both child depths and add one.
maximum-depth-of-binary-tree.explanation: Each node is visited once and recursion uses tree height.

hints: Corresponding nodes must agree in existence and value.
Compare both trees recursively in lockstep.
Two null nodes match; one null or unequal values fail; otherwise compare left pairs and right pairs.
same-tree.explanation: Each corresponding node pair is checked once with recursion depth h.

hints: Null positions must be represented to preserve shape.
Preorder traversal with a null marker is self-delimiting.
Serialize value,left,right; deserialize by consuming tokens in the same order, returning null at the marker.
serialize-and-deserialize-binary-tree.explanation: Both operations process one token per node or null child and build proportional output.

hints: A subtree match can begin at any node with the same value.
Use one helper for whole-tree equality and another to search candidate roots.
At each main-tree node, return true if sameTree(node,subRoot), otherwise search the left and right children.
subtree-of-another-tree.explanation: In the worst case an O(n) equality check begins at O(m) nodes; recursion uses tree height.

hints: Each node is constrained by all of its ancestors, not just its parent.
Carry an exclusive lower and upper bound down recursion.
Require lower < node.val < upper; recurse left with upper=node.val and right with lower=node.val.
validate-binary-search-tree.explanation: Every node is checked once and recursion depth is the tree height.

hints: Many words share prefixes, so search them together.
Build a trie, then backtrack from board cells while following trie edges.
When a trie node marks a word, record it once; mark board cells during DFS and prune exhausted trie branches.
word-search-ii.explanation: Trie-guided backtracking bounds each path by maximum word length and stores all prefixes.

hints: Keep the lower and upper halves balanced.
Use a max-heap for the lower half and min-heap for the upper half.
Insert into the appropriate heap, rebalance sizes to differ by at most one, then read one top or average both tops.
find-median-from-data-stream.explanation: Each insertion performs heap operations and all streamed values remain stored.

hints: Count first, then select by frequency rather than value.
Bucket indices can represent frequencies from 1 through n.
Place each value in bucket[count], then scan buckets downward until k values are collected.
top-k-frequent-elements.explanation: Counting and bucket scanning are linear and store all distinct values.
